setup: Merton model, non-dividend-paying firm, debt due in $T = 10$ years. An analyst has computed $d_1 = 2.321$ and $d_2 = 2.143$. Asset volatility is assumed constant.
ask: The implied asset volatility $\sigma_V$ is closest to:

options.why: Divided the gap by $T = 10$ instead of $\sqrt{T}$: $0.178/10 = 1.78\%$.
Stopped at $d_1 - d_2 = 0.178$ and read it as the volatility, forgetting that the gap is $\sigma_V\sqrt{T}$, not $\sigma_V$.
Multiplied the gap by $\sqrt{10}$ instead of dividing: $0.178 \times 3.162 = 0.563$.

takeaway: The gap $d_1 - d_2$ is $\sigma_V\sqrt{T}$, so divide it by $\sqrt{T}$. Over a 10-year horizon the annual volatility is about a third of the gap.

setup: A firm has assets of USD 110m and a single zero-coupon bond, face USD 80m, due in 5 years. The risk-free rate is 4% (continuous). The BSM put on the firm's assets struck at 80 is worth USD 6.95m. The riskless present value of the debt is $80e^{-0.04 \times 5} = 65.50$.
ask: The market value of the firm's (risky) debt is:

options.label: Above USD 65.50m
options.why: Added the put to the riskless value ($65.50 + 6.95 = 72.45$). Creditors are short the default put, so it reduces what the debt is worth.

options.label: Equal to USD 65.50m
options.why: Treated the debt as riskless. The firm can default, and that risk is what the put prices.

takeaway: Risky debt = riskless debt minus the default put. Creditors are short that put, so debt always sits below its riskless value.

setup: Merton model, firm value USD 100.0m. Senior debt (face 60) and subordinated debt (face 40) are both 5-year zero-coupon bonds. Equity is a call struck at total debt: $c(100, 100, 5) = 24.33$. A call struck at the senior face only is $c(100, 60, 5) = 49.33$.
ask: The value of the subordinated debt is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 2.5m
options.why: Scale slip (0.1×).

options.label: ≈ USD 76m
options.why: Took $V - E = 100 - 24.33 = 75.67$, which is ALL the debt, and never took the senior claim out of it.

options.label: ≈ USD 250m
options.why: Scale slip (10×). It is worth more than the whole firm.

takeaway: Firm value splits three ways: equity + senior + subordinated = V. Subordinated is what is left after equity and senior are taken out.

setup: Merton model. Firm assets are USD 240m and equity is USD 150m, with equity volatility $\sigma_E = 30\%$. $N(d_1) = 0.95$. Ito's lemma links the two volatilities: $\sigma_E E_0 = N(d_1)\,\sigma_V V_0$.
ask: Compared with the 30% equity volatility, the asset volatility $\sigma_V$ is:

options.label: Higher
options.why: Inverted the leverage ratio, using $V_0/E_0 = 1.6$ in place of $E_0/V_0$: $0.30 \times 240/(150 \times 0.95) = 50.5\%$. Equity sits on top of debt, so it is the more volatile claim.

options.label: The same
options.why: Assumed $E_0 = V_0$ and $N(d_1) = 1$ (no debt, no leverage). Here debt is 90m, so equity is a levered claim.

takeaway: Equity is a levered call on assets, so $\sigma_E > \sigma_V$. The asset volatility is $\sigma_E$ scaled down by $E_0/V_0$ and up by $1/N(d_1)$.

setup: Merton model: assets $V_0 = 120$, one-year zero-coupon debt of face 100, $r = 3\%$ (continuous), $\sigma_V = 44\%$. Given $N(d_1) = 0.7588$ and $N(d_2) = 0.6036$. The riskless present value of the debt is $100e^{-0.03} = 97.04$.
ask: The value of equity, the call $V_0 N(d_1) - 97.04\,N(d_2)$, is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 3.2m
options.why: Scale slip (0.1×).

options.label: ≈ USD 9.5m
options.why: Reported the value of the default put ($97.04 \times 0.3964 - 120 \times 0.2412 = 9.53$) as the equity.

options.label: ≈ USD 91m
options.why: Stopped after the first term, $120 \times 0.7588 = 91.06$, and never subtracted the discounted-strike term.

takeaway: Equity is a call on the assets: a large first term less a large second term. The two are close in size, so the answer is much smaller than either.

setup: Merton model, firm debt maturing in $T = 5$ years, constant asset volatility. The software reports $d_1 = 3.217790$ and $d_2 = 3.038905$. Equity is USD 45m and debt USD 60m.

options.label: Between 10% and 30%
options.why: Read the gap $d_1 - d_2 = 0.179$ as the volatility itself ($17.9\%$), forgetting the $\sqrt{T}$.

options.label: Above 30%
options.why: Multiplied the gap by $\sqrt{5}$ instead of dividing: $0.179 \times 2.236 = 40\%$.

takeaway: $d_1 - d_2 = \sigma_V\sqrt{T}$ only. The equity and debt values are not needed.

setup: ICB Corp: assets GBP 25bn, asset volatility 45%, expected asset return 8%, risk-free 3%. Treat GBP 10bn of debt as one zero-coupon liability due in one year. You are building the real-world distance to default $DD = [\ln(V/D) + (\mu - \sigma^2/2)T]/(\sigma\sqrt{T})$.

options.label: Positive
options.why: Saw $\mu = 8\%$ and assumed a positive drift. The $\sigma^2/2$ term is $0.45^2/2 = 10.1\%$, which is larger than 8%.

takeaway: With high volatility, $\sigma^2/2$ can exceed the expected return, so the drift in $DD$ can be negative. The $\ln(V/D)$ term still carries the result.

setup: Logos International: assets USD 280m, debt face USD 478m due in 7 years. Expected asset return 18%, asset volatility 21%. Debt is larger than assets today. Default probability at maturity is $N(-d_2)$ with $d_2 = [\ln(V/D) + (\mu - \sigma^2/2)T]/(\sigma\sqrt{T})$.
ask: The probability of default at maturity is:

options.label: Above 50%
options.why: Looked only at $\ln(280/478) = -0.535$ (assets below debt) and ignored the seven years of drift, $+1.106$, which flips the numerator positive.

takeaway: Over a long horizon the drift term can outweigh a negative $\ln(V/D)$. A positive $d_2$ always means a default probability below 50%.

setup: Company X has assets of USD 1.3m and must repay USD 1.0m of debt in three months. Expected asset return 15% a year, asset volatility 30% a year. Real-world default probability is $N(-d_2)$.
ask: The probability of default over the three months is closest to:

options.why: Used $\sigma T = 0.075$ instead of $\sigma\sqrt{T} = 0.15$ in the denominator, so $d_2$ balloons to 3.85.
Dropped the three-month horizon and used $T = 1$: $d_2 = 1.22$, $PD = N(-1.22)$.
Read $N(d_2)$ (the survival probability) instead of $N(-d_2)$.

takeaway: Short horizon: both the drift and the denominator shrink with $T$ (as $T$ and $\sqrt{T}$). Convert 3 months to $T = 0.25$ before anything else.

setup: Assets USD 62m, asset volatility 38%, one-year zero-coupon debt of face USD 40m. Risk-free rate 2%; expected asset return 10%. You compute two default probabilities: $N(-d_2)$ with the drift $r$ (risk-neutral) and $N(-d_2)$ with the drift $\mu$ (real-world).
ask: The risk-neutral default probability, compared with the real-world one, is:

options.label: Lower
options.why: Thought the lower rate means a safer firm. A lower drift shrinks $d_2$ (here 1.02 against 1.23), and a smaller distance to default means a higher default probability.

options.label: The same
options.why: Assumed the drift is irrelevant. It enters the numerator of $d_2$ directly, so $r \ne \mu$ gives different probabilities.

takeaway: A lower drift gives a smaller $d_2$ and a higher PD. Risk-neutral PDs (drift $r$) exceed real-world PDs (drift $\mu$) whenever $\mu > r$.

setup: Vasicek model for a granular USD 100m retail book: PD = 2.0%, recovery 50%, copula correlation $\rho = 0.13$, 99.9% confidence. $N^{-1}(0.02) = -2.054$, $N^{-1}(0.999) = 3.090$. $WCDR = N\!\left(\frac{N^{-1}(PD) + \sqrt{\rho}\,N^{-1}(X)}{\sqrt{1-\rho}}\right)$.
ask: The worst-case default rate (WCDR) is closest to:

options.why: Took the worst-case rate to be the PD itself. The whole point of the 99.9% shock is that it pushes the default rate far above the average.
Used $\rho$ in place of $\sqrt{\rho}$ (0.13 against 0.36), which understates the shock: $N(-1.77) = 3.8\%$.
Left out the $\sqrt{\rho}$ weight and added the full $N^{-1}(0.999) = 3.09$: $N(1.11) = 86.7\%$.

takeaway: A 2% PD turns into a roughly 16% worst-case default rate at 99.9% with $\rho = 0.13$. Credit VaR is then WCDR $\times$ EAD $\times$ LGD.

setup: A bank must post collateral worth USD 30m after haircuts. Haircuts: cash 0%, government bonds 2%, corporate bonds 4%. It posts USD 10m of cash, all USD 12m of government bonds, then enough corporate bonds to cover the rest.
ask: The total MARKET value of collateral posted is:

options.label: Exactly USD 30m
options.why: Ignored the haircuts and matched market value to the requirement. Haircuts cut the credit, so more market value is needed.

options.label: Below USD 30m
options.why: Applied the haircut in the wrong direction, as if the posted value could exceed the credit. The credit is below market value, so market value must be above the credit.

takeaway: A haircut makes credit smaller than market value. To land on a fixed credit you must post more than that in market value.

setup: A bank must post collateral worth USD 45m after haircuts. It posts in order: USD 10m cash (haircut 0%), USD 15m of 4-year Treasuries (2%), USD 20m of 4-year corporate bonds (4%), then gold (15%) for any shortfall. Market values of the first three add to exactly 45.
ask: After cash, Treasuries and corporates, the credit received is:

options.label: Below USD 45m, so gold is still needed
Exactly USD 45m, so the call is met
options.why: Added market values (10 + 15 + 20 = 45) instead of post-haircut credit. The requirement is on the credited amount.

options.label: Above USD 45m
options.why: Applied the haircuts as if they added to value. A haircut can only reduce the credit.

takeaway: Check the requirement against credit (after haircuts), never against market value. The shortfall must be topped up with the next asset, grossed up for its own haircut.

setup: One-way CSA: only the hedge fund posts. Threshold USD 65m, minimum transfer amount (MTA) USD 12m, collateral already held USD 50m. The net exposure has risen to USD 110m. Credit support amount = max(exposure - threshold, 0) - collateral held.

options.label: Positive
options.why: Ignored the threshold and compared exposure with collateral: $110 - 50 = +60$. The threshold of 65 comes off first.

working.label: Result
working.display: Negative: no additional collateral to post (and $|5| < \text{MTA} = 12$ anyway)

takeaway: Collateral is only required above the threshold. A negative credit support amount means over-collateralised, and nothing is called.

setup: One-way CSA: the hedge fund posts. Threshold CNY 14.0m, minimum transfer amount (MTA) CNY 2.5m, collateral already held CNY 10.8m. The net exposure rises to CNY 27.0m.
ask: The credit support amount, compared with the MTA, is:

options.label: Below the MTA, so no call is made
Above the MTA, so a call is made
options.why: Ignored the threshold: $27.0 - 10.8 = 16.2$, far above 2.5. The threshold of 14.0 comes off the exposure first.

takeaway: Check the MTA after the threshold: a call below the MTA is simply not made, so the extra collateral is zero.
